batch_strategy: Select 16 supplements testing solvent-response shape, structural transfer within alcohol and carbonyl families, and one loading-protocol interaction. Preserve all supplied premeasurement predictions and freeze these selections together with the 16 pending experiments before any new label reveal.

choices.reason: Measure m128 at 20/1, 50 uL, predicted approximately 30.79/49.49 mL. Measured 5/1 and 10/1 at 150 uL increased from 19.39/38.45 to 33.83/57.29 (91cd087e44e7a3364533, 596bd04bfe916866f908), whereas this weaker-eluent prediction falls below the 10/1 observation. Test whether the apparent reversal is real or a response-shape failure. The sample-load difference remains a competing explanation.

Measure m40 at 50/1, 50 uL, predicted approximately 16.60/35.23 mL. Its newly measured 20/1, 100-uL row b645df00945e594953a6 gave 20.33/37.51 after underprediction. The weaker-eluent forecast is slightly earlier despite that anchor. This tests whether retraining learned only a local correction for acetylnaphthalene; loading differs and remains a competing explanation.

Measure m205 at 1/1, 100 uL, predicted approximately 11.32/25.53 mL. Same-load measurements at 2/1 and 5/1 were 27.63/51.49 and 51.43/98.38 (c973d4c257be9ef08216, 48853fd78c77153b963a). The 2/1 label remained substantially underpredicted after the 5/1 anchor. This stronger-eluent point locates the rise and tests whether retention is compressed across the alcohol response.

Measure m204 at 10/1, 100 uL, predicted approximately 46.96/80.30 mL. The recent same-load 5/1 result b7b1a1bb666c8cc99bad was accurately predicted at 28.62/51.27, following measured 2/1 retention of 13.06/22.22 (53c1be5b96937954b9fa). This tests whether successful interpolation extends to weaker eluent and connects a simple primary alcohol to the naphthyl alcohols.

Measure secondary alcohol m60 at 10/1, 100 uL, predicted approximately 34.77/59.81 mL. Its measured 1/1, 150-uL anchor c5594361764ec76761e2 is 5.02/14.92. Related tertiary alcohol m51 measured 37.67/57.93 at 10/1, 50 uL (4fb92bd1fab3ba235858). Together with selected primary alcohol m204, this tests whether similar predictions conceal differences in hydroxyl substitution and accessibility; cross-molecule loading differences remain covariates.

Measure tertiary benzylic alcohol m203 at 10/1, 50 uL, predicted approximately 23.46/29.05 mL. Its same-load 20/1 observation 9ed7c1fb1c2cc499bbf9 was 37.76/44.96, while 5/1 at 150 uL was 9.52/14.71 (eb151126b40eda411ab7). This intermediate point tests the predicted onset rise with a relatively short elution interval, contrasting broader primary-alcohol responses.

Measure m173 in pure EA with 1500-uL DCM loading, predicted approximately 4.71/50.49 mL. The approximately mass-matched 2000-uL pure-EA row 6802f0b28c5a0c7b4c2a gave 5.12/50.30. At 1/1 the protocols finished at 78.37 and 108.89 mL (65fcce0299e031dedeb8, f90a5a5a54509c085ebd), although their 5/1 completions were similar. This tests whether the 1/1 protocol difference persists in stronger eluent; a single comparison cannot exclude variability.

Measure previously unobserved m49 at 50/1, 50 uL, predicted approximately 5.72/18.97 mL. Its maximum similarity to observed molecules is 0.364. This bulky alkyl-substituted aromatic aldehyde tests transfer to a low-polarity structural environment without assuming direct ortho shielding. Measured dimethylbenzaldehyde 23e0c45fe7c2db0d34ba provides a related 20/1 anchor but does not establish this new molecule's response.

Measure previously unobserved bromonaphthaldehyde m196 at 20/1, 100 uL, predicted approximately 14.02/33.23 mL. Unbrominated naphthaldehyde m195 measured 9.98/25.87 at the same ratio and sample volume (783cf2454912fc14bb80); acetylnaphthalene m40 measured 20.33/37.51 (b645df00945e594953a6). This tests structural ordering across fused aromatic carbonyls. Density and loading volume differ, so the contrast is not exclusively structural.

Measure previously unobserved para-bromoacetophenone m30 at 50/1, 100 uL, predicted approximately 12.56/28.70 mL. Recent weak-eluent labels for para-methylacetophenone and fluoro-propiophenone were earlier than acquisition predictions (485f8bcfb08d6eaf3463, 5307ce95bcee2886afe0), while m40 showed the opposite error. This adds a connected halogenated ketone and tests substituent transfer without imposing a uniform carbonyl correction.

Measure previously unobserved ortho-tolualdehyde m145 at 20/1, 100 uL, predicted approximately 8.40/22.50 mL. Meta-tolualdehyde at 20/1, 150 uL measured 5.32/24.75 (ca28db10589bf3ee4600); dimethylbenzaldehyde at 20/1, 50 uL gave 7.70/18.45 (23e0c45fe7c2db0d34ba). This tests positional-substitution transfer in a simple scaffold, with loading differences preventing a pure positional-isomer inference.

Measure lactone m181 at 50/1, 150 uL, predicted approximately 22.62/38.47 mL. Its same-load 10/1 observation 64c9e190e213bb061867 was already 17.98/32.13. The forecast implies only a modest increase across a large reduction in eluent strength. This tests whether a plateau transfers from some cyclic ketones or the lactone has an unlearned late rise.

Measure para-nitroacetophenone m37 at 20/1, 100 uL, predicted approximately 40.44/78.36 mL. The same-load 10/1 observation 38e6b8bf0f089fcadd80 was 25.64/55.08. Pending m177 at 20/1 supplies a nitrobenzophenone contrast, and pending m37 at 1/1 supplies a strong-eluent endpoint. This tests the predicted steep rise and distinction between acetophenone and benzophenone.

Measure multifunctional ester m13 at 10/1, 150 uL, predicted approximately 23.20/54.67 mL. Its same-load 5/1 measurement 5d530b2f228ed39ff952 was 17.85/43.86; pending m13 at 1/1 extends the same protocol toward stronger eluent. This adds a response segment for an ester/ketone/ether-rich molecule and tests whether completion rises more sharply than forecast.

Measure ortho-nitrobenzaldehyde m198 at 20/1, 150 uL, predicted approximately 25.92/62.05 mL. Same-load measurements bracket it: 14.38/36.06 at 10/1 and 40.78/94.30 at 50/1 (e99da719af7e2c3e9a93, 0ac58929e586a4da4056). The former was predicted reasonably, while the latter had a 33.37-mL completion underprediction. This clean intermediate contrast locates response acceleration and connects to the para-isomer series.

Measure ethyl anisate m87 at 20/1, 50 uL, predicted approximately 18.74/39.47 mL. Its same-load 50/1 anchor 810b16f35a3a86f451ce is 24.51/49.53; 10/1 at 150 uL was 7.31/21.79 (ef809aee1c6b06021475). This tests whether a late anchor has moved the predicted rise too early, a failure seen recently in m178 and m129, while extending that question to aromatic esters.

hypotheses.content: Solvent-response errors often concern the location and endpoint-specific shape of a retention rise rather than a constant molecule-level offset. A late anchor can coexist with substantial overprediction at intermediate PE/EA ratios.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: Labels on response segments can correct neighboring conditions and teach separate V1 and V2 behavior. They can prevent late-retention anchors from inducing premature rises throughout a chemical family.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Does m198 follow its predicted intermediate rise, does m128 truly reverse at 20/1, and do m87 and m181 rise earlier or later than forecast?

hypotheses.content: Alcohol retention and solvent-response shape depend on hydroxyl placement, substitution, and aromatic environment. The naphthylethanol failure does not imply that all aromatic alcohol predictions require the same correction.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: The selected primary, secondary, and tertiary alcohols test whether the representation distinguishes local hydroxyl environments and predicts onset and completion separately across related rows.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Does m205 remain unexpectedly retained at 1/1, and do the predicted 10/1 responses of m204, m60, and m203 preserve their different interval widths?

hypotheses.content: Aromatic carbonyls need structure-dependent response models: fused rings, aldehyde versus ketone identity, and substituent placement can alter retention substantially. A universal upward correction after a weak-eluent failure would transfer poorly.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: Recent carbonyl acquisitions show both error signs. Chemically connected new molecules can distinguish transferable structural effects from corrections specific to a previously measured molecule.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Are the low predictions for m49 and moderate predictions for m196, m30, and m145 justified, and does m40 continue to increase beyond 20/1?

hypotheses.content: Loading-protocol effects are conditional and may be confounded with experimental variability. Cinnamic acid shows a substantial completion difference between its two 1/1 protocols, whereas the corresponding 5/1 protocols and m72's two 10/1 protocols are much closer.
hypotheses.why_it_matters_for_model_learning: An additional protocol contrast tests interaction with mobile phase without encouraging a universal loading-volume correction. The recorded densities are only approximately mass matched for m173.
hypotheses.next_discriminating_question: Do the two m173 loading volumes give similar completion in pure EA, as predicted, or does the difference observed at 1/1 persist?

feedback_interpretation: The latest outcomes strengthen response-shape repair but weaken blanket expectations of high retention. m178 at 10/1 measured 6.24/27.45, below its acquisition prediction, placing its major rise later than forecast. m129's predicted reversal was rejected: measured 10/1 endpoints were 10.18/24.26, far earlier than its measured 50/1 endpoints. Conversely, m114 at 20/1 and m128 at 5/1 were reasonably predicted, reducing the priority of further loading replication there. m205 at 2/1 still showed substantial underprediction, while m204 at 5/1 was accurate; this favors structural and solvent comparisons within alcohols. m40 was underpredicted, m176 overpredicted, and m63 only modestly underpredicted, weakening any uniform correction for aromatic ketones. Both m15 labels rejected its predicted steep retention rise, and its current forecasts are closer to those observations. m120's low-load late onset also occurred at 2/1, but its irregular 5/1 midpoint still prevents a smooth universal loading interpretation. m72's two 10/1 protocols gave nearly identical completion. m173 retained a broad interval at 1/1 with 1500-uL loading, but completion was about 30.53 mL earlier than with 2000 uL, making its pure-EA comparison discriminating. The inconsistent endpoint ordering in m117's 10/1 label remains unresolved and does not establish a physical negative-width mechanism.
batch_rationale: The pending 16 already cover aromatic esters, nitro carbonyls, salicylaldehyde, one new halogenated aromatic molecule, and strong-eluent conditions. These supplements add response segments around measured failures, connected exploration of four unobserved carbonyl molecules, a comparative alcohol set, and one loading-volume contrast. Same-load solvent comparisons are used where available; the m128 and m40 tests retain loading as a competing explanation. The batch avoids duplicate pending tuples and repeated confirmation of already accurate loading contrasts. The m198 intermediate point, m205 strong-eluent point, and tests of apparent m128/m40 reversals address different ways late anchors can fail to generalize. New carbonyls and alcohol comparisons test transfer to neighboring structures across the Row-distribution. Quantile widths remain uncalibrated outputs of one predictor, with zero V1 lower quantiles and crossings discouraging width-only ranking. Expected value comes from teaching structure-condition relationships for both endpoints, with variability and absent protocol variables limiting mechanistic interpretation.
